true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BuildIndex can run concurrently for the same namespaced resource

The patch removes the global lock around BuildIndex but adds no per-key synchronization or singleflight. GetIndex returns nil until BuildIndex inserts the finished index, so concurrent Search or watch-event calls for the same namespace/group/resource can both start builds. This duplicates work, can open the same file-backed bleve directory concurrently, and lets the last writer replace another live index in the cache without closing it. Add a per-key lock or reserve the key while building.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race: narrowing the cache lock allows concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key to duplicate expensive index construction. The candidate adds consequences and mitigation but matches the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the index cache without locking

bleveBackend.TotalDocs ranges over b.cache while BuildIndex may concurrently write to that map. TotalDocs does not take cacheMu.RLock, so this is an unsynchronized map read/write that can panic or return wrong totals. This is more likely now that BuildIndex only locks for the cache insertion.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same unsynchronized access to b.cache: TotalDocs iterates the map while concurrent BuildIndex calls may write to it, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic. The candidate omits the event watcher context but matches the underlying bug.

false_positives.candidate:
Unsynchronized shared writes in search init workers

searchSupport.init starts multiple errgroup workers that all increment totalBatchesIndexed and assign to the outer err variable. These are shared variables with no mutex, atomic, or local handling, so concurrent index builds race. The reported indexed count can be wrong, an error can be overwritten, and the Go race detector will fail.

History and Origin dereference s.search without nil checks

server.History calls s.search.History and server.Origin calls s.search.Origin, but s.search can be nil when search is not configured. server.Search checks for this case, while History and Origin will panic on a nil pointer if invoked. Add nil checks or return a not-configured error.

Watch loop does not handle closed event channel

The goroutine started in searchSupport.init receives from events with v := <-events and passes v to handleEvent. If the storage backend closes the channel, the receive returns a nil *WrittenEvent repeatedly, and handleEvent dereferences evt.Type, causing a panic. The loop also has no context.Done branch, so it cannot be stopped cleanly. Use v, ok := <-events and stop when !ok, and select on a cancellable context.

IndexMetrics is used without nil checks in handleEvent

handleEvent increments and decrements IndexMetrics.IndexedKinds for added and deleted events without checking whether IndexMetrics is nil. Other parts of the code guard with if IndexMetrics != nil. If metrics are not initialized, any ADDED or DELETED watch event will panic.

BuildIndex uses IndexMetrics without nil check

BuildIndex increments resource.IndexMetrics.IndexTenants unconditionally. Since other code paths check whether IndexMetrics is nil, this can panic when metrics are disabled or uninitialized. Guard the metric calls or guarantee initialization.

Constructor leaks context/lifecycle resources when Init fails

NewResourceServer creates a cancellable context and may run lifecycle initialization before s.Init. If s.Init returns an error, the constructor returns without calling cancel or stopping lifecycle hooks, leaking the context and any initialized backend resources. Clean up on the error path.

Initial index build can miss events written before the watch starts

searchSupport.init builds all indexes first and only then calls WatchWriteEvents. Writes that happen while the initial build is running are not included in the built index and are not replayed by the watcher, which starts after the build. In deployments with concurrent writers or other instances, the search index can remain stale until affected resources are written again.

Postgres storage-server integration test is skipped

The test now skips for GRAFANA_TEST_DB=postgres, so the storage server startup path is not exercised against Postgres in CI. Since this PR changes initialization timing and index building, this reduces coverage for a supported database; the skip should be tied to a tracked fix rather than left as an indefinite TODO.

true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same outdated evaluate docstring: it claims to return a list of DetectorEvaluationResult, while the method now returns a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey.

false_positives.candidate:
get_state_data raises KeyError when counter_names is empty

In StatefulDetectorHandler.get_state_data, counter_updates is initialized to {} and only populated if self.counter_names is truthy. Later DetectorStateData is constructed with counter_updates[gk] for every group key. If a subclass legitimately has counter_names == [], this raises KeyError for the first group key, making such a stateful detector unusable. Use a default mapping such as counter_updates.get(gk, {}) or always populate defaults for every requested group key.

Dedupe marker is advanced before validating condition group

evaluate_group_key_value calls enqueue_dedupe_update(group_key, dedupe_value) before checking self.condition_group. process_detectors later calls commit_state_updates even when evaluate returns no results, so a packet that was skipped because the detector has no condition group still persists the new dedupe value. If the missing condition group is temporary or corrected later, that packet will never be re-evaluated, potentially losing alert transitions. The dedupe update should probably only be committed after the packet has actually been evaluated, or at least not when skipping for invalid configuration.

Occurrences are emitted before state updates are committed

process_detectors calls create_issue_occurrence_from_result for every result and only afterwards calls handler.commit_state_updates(). If producing one of the occurrences or the subsequent state commit fails, the dedupe/state changes are not persisted. On retry the same packet will be evaluated again, and any occurrences already produced before the failure can be emitted again. Since this PR makes detector handlers produce real IssueOccurrence/StatusChangeMessage payloads, this path can create duplicate issues unless occurrence identifiers are guaranteed idempotent.

StatefulDetectorHandler.get_group_key_values is annotated as returning dict[str, int], but DetectorGroupKey is used throughout as an optional key and the tests pass {None: ...}. In TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe, the test evaluates evaluate_group_key_value with group_key 'group_key', but the expected occurrence is built with build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, 'val1', ...), giving it a fingerprint for 'val1'. If IssueOccurrence equality includes fingerprint, this test will fail; if equality ignores fingerprint, the test does not verify that the produced occurrence corresponds to the evaluated group key. should_sync returns False whenever sync_source.integration_id matches the installation's integration, regardless of which external issue triggered the inbound change. Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.

false_positives.candidate:
Strategy shuts down the shared FixedQueuePool, breaking later strategy instances

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), but the pool is created by ResultsStrategyFactory and is shared across strategies. Arroyo may close a strategy during a rebalance and then create a new strategy from the same factory. Once close() has shut down the shared pool, worker threads are stopped and queues are closed, so the next strategy will submit to a dead pool. Its submit() exception handler can then mark offsets complete without processing. This can silently drop messages after any rebalance. The strategy should not shut down a factory-owned pool, or a new pool should be created per strategy.

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join() simply calls close(), ignoring the timeout argument. close() stops the commit thread before queue_pool.shutdown() drains remaining queued items, and it never waits for queues or outstanding offsets to become empty. As a result, work processed during shutdown may never have its offsets committed, and shutdown can still block for fixed internal timeouts rather than respecting the requested join timeout.

Shutdown flag can cause queued work items to be dropped

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown = True before allowing queues to drain. OrderedQueueWorker.run() loops on while not self.shutdown, so if a worker is processing an item when shutdown begins it will exit after that one item even if its queue still contains pending work. Although q.shutdown(immediate=False) is intended to permit graceful draining, the worker flag prevents that and can discard queued messages without processing or committing them.

Failed work items are marked complete and become eligible for commit

OrderedQueueWorker.run() catches exceptions from the result processor and still calls offset_tracker.complete_offset() in the finally block. ResultProcessor.__call__ also swallows exceptions. Therefore a result that fails processing is treated as completed and can be committed, despite the strategy documentation saying offsets are committed only after successful processing. A transient failure, such as a database or downstream outage, can permanently lose results with no retry or DLQ.

OffsetTracker iterates shared partition dictionary while other threads may add partitions

OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets() iterates list(self.all_offsets.keys()) without a global lock, while add_offset() may concurrently create new partition entries in self.all_offsets from the submit thread. This can cause dictionary-changed-size-during-iteration errors or missed partitions in the commit loop. Per-partition locks protect individual offset sets but do not protect the partition key collection itself.

Unbounded queues provide no backpressure despite documented guarantee

FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() instances with no maxsize and submit() puts work unconditionally. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.poll() only emits metrics and never applies backpressure. The class documentation claims natural backpressure when queues fill up, but unbounded queues never fill. If workers are slower than the consumer, messages and full Kafka payloads will accumulate in memory without bound and can OOM the process.

FilteredPayload is handled through the generic exception path

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() passes FilteredPayload messages to the decoder. When used with ResultsStrategyFactory.decode_payload(), that decoder asserts the payload is not FilteredPayload, causing an AssertionError that is caught by the generic except branch and logged as 'Error submitting message to queue'. This turns normal filtered messages into exception log spam and relies on exception handling for control flow. FilteredPayload should be explicitly treated as a skipped/completed offset before decoding.

Error-handling test is flaky and asserts behavior opposite to the implementation

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling mocks the result processor to raise for the first message and then asserts that no offsets were committed. However, the worker catches processing exceptions and marks the failed offset complete, so once the commit loop ticks the implementation will commit past the failed message. The test only waits briefly and may pass or fail depending on whether the 1-second commit loop runs before the assertion. It does not reliably validate the intended behavior and masks the fact that failed items are committed.

The comment stating that the ORM handles boundary conditions is incorrect; this will cause exceptions or undefined pagination behavior.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key calls math.floor/math.ceil directly on the ordered field value, and value_from_cursor returns the raw cursor value. In organization_auditlogs.py it is used with order_by='-datetime'. For any non-empty result page, math.ceil(datetime) raises TypeError, and for non-zero cursors the WHERE clause would compare a datetime column to a numeric value. The optimized audit-log pagination path is therefore broken.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key applies math.floor/math.ceil to a datetime value when order_by='-datetime', causing a TypeError. The additional cursor comparison concern does not change the match.

false_positives.candidate:
Unguarded access to organization_context.member may raise AttributeError

The code accesses organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking whether organization_context.member is None. If a request has an organization context without a member, this will raise AttributeError and return a 500 instead of denying access or falling back safely.

New optimized pagination path is untested

The PR adds a new optimized_pagination query-parameter branch and uses OptimizedCursorPaginator, but no tests cover this endpoint behavior or the new paginator. Given the datetime incompatibility and negative-offset handling, this is a high-risk untested code path.

Switch from Redis sets to sorted sets is not backward compatible with in-flight data

Existing span-buf:s:* keys created by the previous code are Redis sets. The new code uses ZADD here, and the Lua script uses ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE, while flushing uses ZSCAN. During a rollout, pre-existing set-typed keys will cause WRONGTYPE errors, causing span buffering or flushing to fail until those keys expire. This needs a migration strategy, dual-type handling, or a new key namespace.

ZUNIONSTORE default SUM aggregation can corrupt span scores

ZUNIONSTORE defaults to AGGREGATE SUM. If the same span payload exists in both the destination and source sorted sets, for example due to duplicate delivery, retries, or overlapping buffer keys, its score becomes the sum of end_timestamp_precise values rather than the original timestamp. This corrupts eviction ordering. The union should use an explicit aggregation such as MAX or MIN.

Eviction can silently drop spans, including root spans, while preserving has-root state

The script evicts the lowest-scored members with ZPOPMIN when a segment exceeds 1000 spans. There is no metric or explicit signal that data was dropped. If the evicted member is the root span, the has_root_span key may still be set because is_root_span was observed, causing the segment to be flushed with root-based timing while missing its root span. This can produce incomplete or inconsistent trace segments.

Reduced redirect-following limit may fragment deep traces

The redirect traversal loop was reduced from 10000 to 1000. If a trace has a redirect chain longer than 1000, new spans will stop at an intermediate redirect target and be stored under the wrong set key, fragmenting the segment. The PR provides no migration or test coverage for this behavioral change.

Consumer hard-fails if end_timestamp_precise is missing

The consumer now reads val['end_timestamp_precise'] directly. If an incoming span message omits this field or provides null due to schema drift, older producers, or malformed data, the consumer will raise KeyError or later fail when using the value as a Redis score. This makes the consumer fragile to upstream variations.

No tests cover the new eviction behavior or sorted-set migration

The core behavioral changes in this PR are the switch from sets to sorted sets and eviction of segments above 1000 spans, but the tests only add end_timestamp_precise values. There is no coverage for segments exceeding the span cap, eviction order, root-span eviction, stale queue entries, or compatibility with old set-typed Redis keys.

false_positives.candidate:
Accidental submodule/gitlink added

The PR adds a gitlink/submodule (`Subproject commit ...`) at repository root. This is unrelated to the feature and can break checkouts/builds or accidentally vendor another repository. It should be removed.

`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` caches allowlist eligibility for 60 seconds, but nothing invalidates these keys when `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` changes. The unused `invalidate_upsampling_cache` helper also only deletes one exact project-set key. `_is_error_focused_query` treats any occurrence of `event.type:error` in the raw query as an error-only query. This matches negated filters like `!event.type:error`, OR clauses that also include transactions, and text/tag values. For discover queries this can replace `count()` with `upsampled_count()` when non-error events are included, producing wrong counts.

upsampled_count is exposed as a public aggregate

The new `upsampled_count` SnQL function is not marked `private=True`, unlike neighboring internal functions. API callers may be able to request it directly, bypassing the allowlist/eligibility logic that only rewrites `count()`, and get incorrect results on projects or datasets where sample weights should not be used.

upsampled_count does not handle missing sample_weight

`upsampled_count` is implemented as `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. If any queried event has NULL/missing `sample_weight` (for example historical events before upsampling was enabled, malformed events, or non-error rows accidentally included in discover), the aggregation can ignore those rows or return NULL/zero, silently changing counts. A fallback or explicit row filtering is needed.

`_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns true for the errors dataset, but the PR only registers `upsampled_count` in the discover dataset converter. If those fields contain or depend on `count()`, top-event selection/ordering may use raw counts while returned timeseries use upsampled counts, making rankings and values inconsistent.

Tests miss high-risk upsampling paths

The endpoint tests cover only simple discover queries with explicit `event.type:error`. They do not cover `dataset=errors`, top events, dashboard split queries, negated/ambiguous event.type conditions, direct use of `upsampled_count()`, or cache expiry/invalidation. These are the paths most likely to expose incorrect counts or query failures.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key construction is ambiguous because fields are joined with underscores

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates namespace, userUID, action, name, and parent using '_' as a separator. Dashboard/folder UIDs can contain underscores, so different combinations of name and parent can produce identical cache keys. For example, name='a_b' with parent='c' yields the same key suffix as name='a' with parent='b_c'. Because this cache stores negative authorization decisions, a key collision can cause a denial for one resource/folder combination to be incorrectly applied to another resource. The key should be constructed with unambiguous escaping/encoding or by hashing the separate fields.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify ambiguous underscore-delimited concatenation in userPermDenialCacheKey that can cause key collisions and incorrectly apply cached permission denials to other resources. The candidate provides a concrete example of the same underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key omits identity type, allowing denials to leak between identities

userPermDenialCacheKey is built only from namespace, userUID, action, name, and parent folder. validateSubject permits multiple identity types, and different identities can have the same identifier string. For example, 'anonymous:0' and 'render:0' both parse to userUID "0". If an anonymous check for 'dashboards:read' on a dashboard is denied, the denial is cached under a key like ns.perm_0_dashboards:read_<dash>_. A subsequent renderer check for the same dashboard will hit this denial cache at line 117 and be denied before getRendererPermissions can return its built-in read access. The denial cache key must include the identity type (and ideally a normalized internal identity ID) to avoid cross-identity wrongful denials.

Cached denial can persist after permission is granted

When a permission check reaches the database and denies access, the result is cached in permDenialCache for shortCacheTTL (30 seconds). There is no invalidation when permissions change. If the first check for a newly created dashboard/folder happens before the new permission is visible (for example due to read-replica lag or asynchronous permission provisioning), the denial is cached. Subsequent checks within the TTL hit the denial cache and skip the database requery, leaving the creator unable to access the newly created resource for up to the TTL. This reintroduces the same class of staleness problem the PR is trying to fix.

Tests do not cover denial-cache isolation by identity type or grant-after-denial behavior

TestService_CacheCheck only pre-seeds a denial entry for a user and checks that it denies access. It does not verify that denial entries are scoped by identity type, so it would not catch a denial for anonymous affecting the renderer identity. It also does not verify behavior when a permission is granted after a denial has been cached. Since the denial cache is a new authorization decision path, tests should cover cross-identity isolation and stale-denial scenarios.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unsafe access to metadata['sender']['login'] can cause a 500

GitHubInstallation.dispatch compares the OAuth-authenticated user to integration.metadata['sender']['login']. Many legitimate Integration rows may not have metadata.sender (for example, integrations created before this change, installations where the webhook has not populated sender, or first-pass installations as shown in the tests). In those cases this direct subscripting can raise KeyError or TypeError and return a 500 instead of the intended graceful error page. The code should use safe lookups and fail closed when sender login is missing.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify unchecked access to integration.metadata['sender']['login'] when sender metadata is absent, causing a KeyError rather than graceful handling.

false_positives.candidate:
User mismatch validation is skipped when the Integration row does not exist

The new security check only runs after an Integration row exists. When Integration.DoesNotExist is raised, the view returns pipeline.next_step() without verifying that github_authenticated_user matches the installer. If the installation webhook that records sender is delayed, fails, or has not created/updated the Integration yet, the advertised mismatch validation is bypassed and an installation_id could potentially be completed by a different authenticated GitHub user. The flow should fail closed or otherwise verify installer identity before creating the integration.

Query-string installation_id can override the pipeline-bound installation_id

GitHubInstallation.dispatch uses request.GET.get('installation_id', pipeline.fetch_state('installation_id')), which lets a query-string parameter overwrite any installation_id already stored during the OAuth step. This weakens the binding between the GitHub OAuth identity and the installation ID. If an installation_id has already been bound in pipeline state, the view should use that value or require the query parameter to match it rather than silently allowing it to be swapped.

OAuth token exchange omits redirect_uri

The authorization request includes redirect_uri, but the access-token exchange sends only code, client_id, and client_secret. Omitting redirect_uri prevents Sentry from explicitly binding the code exchange to the callback URL used in the authorize step. This matters if the GitHub OAuth app can have multiple callback URLs or if a code could be obtained through another registered redirect URI. The same redirect_uri should be included in the token exchange.

OAuth exchange and user-info fetch can raise 500 instead of showing the intended error

safe_urlopen and get_user_info are called without exception handling; only parsing the response body is wrapped. Network timeouts, connection errors, HTTP errors, or exceptions raised by get_user_info will bubble up and produce a 500 instead of the intended installation-failed error page. The token exchange and user-info fetch should be wrapped and return error() on failure. Also treat an empty access_token as missing, not merely absent.

Authorize redirect URL is built without URL encoding

The GitHub authorize URL is constructed with an f-string, interpolating client_id, state, and redirect_uri directly into the query string. redirect_uri should be URL-encoded to avoid malformed or rejected URLs when reserved characters are present, and to make the construction robust to future changes. Use urllib.parse.urlencode to build the query parameters.

Redirect can be built with installation_id=None

If GitHub redirects with setup_action=install but without an installation_id, installation_id is None and is passed directly to reverse('integration-installation', args=[provider_id, installation_id]). This can generate a URL containing the literal None or cause a reverse/404 failure. The view should handle a missing installation_id with a graceful redirect or error page.

false_positives.candidate:
Login-cache invalidation can be skipped when the original IDP is resolved through an organization-aware wrapper

In update(), the original model is loaded with getById(), which returns an organization-aware IdentityProviderModel whose isEnabled() is false when the linked organization is disabled. registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate() then applies LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate() to this wrapped original. If the organization is disabled, an update that removes login eligibility (for example hideOnLogin=true, linkOnly=true, or broker.public=false) can be evaluated as false -> false and no login-cache invalidation is registered. When the organization is later enabled, the stale getForLogin cache can still contain the provider, and callers that only re-check isEnabled() may display a hidden, private, or link-only provider. Use the raw delegate model for the original state, or invalidate whenever login-related fields change.

getForLogin cache does not react to organization invalidation

getForLogin() checks only isInvalid(cacheKey), where cacheKey is realm+FetchMode. It stores organization-specific result sets inside that mode-level cache entry using organizationId as a search key, but it does not check organization invalidation or otherwise tie the entry to organization lifecycle changes. getByOrganization() at least checks isInvalid(orgId). As a result, organization changes such as enable/disable or update do not refresh these cached login lists, so stale organization-scoped IDP lists can be returned until an unrelated IDP change invalidates the mode key.

Cached getForLogin results are returned without re-validating login eligibility

In the cached path, getForLogin() resolves each cached internal ID and adds the model to the result without verifying that it still satisfies the login criteria (enabled, not link-only, not hidden, and public when organization-linked). The correctness of the cache therefore depends entirely on invalidations being complete. If an invalidation is missed, for example when an IDP is updated while its organization is disabled, this method can return providers that should no longer be available for login. Filtering cached entries before returning them would prevent stale ineligible providers from being exposed.

Mode-level login cache can accumulate unbounded organization search keys

cacheKeyForLogin() is keyed only by realm and FetchMode, while each distinct organizationId queried is stored as another search key inside the same IdentityProviderListQuery. There is no eviction of individual organization search keys; adding a new one invalidates and replaces the whole entry. In realms with many organizations this cached object can grow large and cause extra invalidation/replication overhead. Consider keying by organization or limiting/evicting search keys.

Possible NullPointerException in remove() for a nonexistent alias

remove() fetches storedIdp from the delegate before deletion. If the alias does not exist and isInvalid(cacheKey) is true, storedIdp is null and registerIDPInvalidation(storedIdp) dereferences it, causing a NullPointerException. This can turn removal of a nonexistent alias into an internal error in some cache states. Guard against a null storedIdp before registering invalidation.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.

Delete success metric uses the object name as the kind label

After a successful unified-storage delete, recordStorageDuration is called with name as the kind label instead of options.Kind. This corrupts the metric's kind dimension and can introduce high-cardinality labels because every object name becomes a separate metric label value. The call should use options.Kind, as in the other methods.

false_positives.candidate:
Asynchronous legacy writes inherit the request context and may be canceled immediately

In Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection, the goroutine that writes to legacy storage derives its context from the incoming request context. When the API request completes, that context is canceled, so the asynchronous legacy create/update/delete/delete-collection can be canceled before it finishes. Mode 3 depends on these asynchronous writes to keep legacy storage in sync, so this can silently drop legacy writes. Use a detached context for the asynchronous operation, preserving only logging/values, not request cancellation.

Legacy update reuses the original UpdatedObjectInfo after it was already used by unified storage

Update calls Storage.Update with the provided rest.UpdatedObjectInfo and then passes the same objInfo to Legacy.Update asynchronously. UpdatedObjectInfo can be request-scoped or one-use, and it may compute the new object from the old object in the store that calls it. Legacy storage may therefore fail, consume an already-consumed payload, or apply the update to a different legacy state, producing a different object than unified storage. For dual-write convergence, legacy should receive the already-updated object returned from Storage.Update, ideally through a wrapper or deep copy.

Delete does not attempt legacy deletion when unified storage returns NotFound

Delete returns immediately if Storage.Delete fails, including when the object is not found in unified storage. In mode 3, legacy storage may still contain a stale copy, and this code path will never clean it up. The previous behavior tolerated NotFound from unified storage and still attempted the legacy delete. Skipping legacy deletion on NotFound can leave divergent legacy objects permanently.

DeleteCollection does not attempt legacy deletion when unified storage returns an error

DeleteCollection returns immediately if Storage.DeleteCollection fails, so Legacy.DeleteCollection is not attempted. If unified storage reports an error or has already removed the collection while legacy storage still contains objects, the legacy data will remain and the stores will diverge. For mode 3 dual-write cleanup, legacy deletion should still be attempted where appropriate, especially when the unified store reports the collection is already absent.

Async legacy create uses the original object without copying it

Create passes the same runtime.Object pointer to the asynchronous Legacy.Create call that was passed to Storage.Create. Storage implementations commonly mutate the object during create, and legacy storage may also mutate it. Returning to the caller while a background goroutine continues to use or mutate the same object can cause data races and inconsistent objects. The object should be deep-copied before being handed to the asynchronous legacy writer.

Storage create failure is recorded as a legacy-store duration

When Storage.Create fails, Create records the duration with recordLegacyDuration using the storage start time. This reports a unified-storage failure under legacy-store metrics, making storage and legacy latency/error metrics incorrect. It should call recordStorageDuration.

Storage update failure is recorded as a legacy-store duration

When Storage.Update fails, Update records the duration with recordLegacyDuration using the storage start time. This mislabels unified-storage update failures as legacy-store update failures. It should call recordStorageDuration.

Legacy delete-collection duration is recorded as a storage duration

In the asynchronous DeleteCollection goroutine, the result of Legacy.DeleteCollection is recorded with recordStorageDuration. This reports legacy-store delete-collection latency/errors under unified-storage metrics. It should call recordLegacyDuration.

Every write starts an unbounded goroutine for legacy replication

Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection each start a new goroutine for the legacy write. There is no queue, worker pool, semaphore, or other backpressure mechanism. If legacy storage is slow or unavailable, write traffic can create a large number of blocked goroutines, increasing memory use and potentially destabilizing the process.

Destroy does not wait for outstanding asynchronous legacy writes

Destroy closes both Storage and Legacy immediately, but mode 3 may still have outstanding goroutines calling Legacy.Create, Legacy.Update, Legacy.Delete, or Legacy.DeleteCollection. Those goroutines can then operate on destroyed storage, causing errors or panics. The dual writer should track outstanding asynchronous writes and wait for them, or at least cancel and drain them, during Destroy.

Asynchronous legacy write failures are not logged

The asynchronous legacy paths only record metrics when the legacy operation fails; they no longer log the error. Since mode 3 returns success to the client as soon as unified storage succeeds, legacy failures are otherwise invisible. This makes diagnosing divergence between unified and legacy storage difficult. Errors from asynchronous legacy writes should be logged, ideally with the object identity and operation.

Unit tests do not synchronize with or verify asynchronous legacy writes

Mode 3 methods start background goroutines, but the unit tests return immediately after calling Create, Delete, Update, or DeleteCollection. There is no WaitGroup, channel, or injectable executor to wait for the legacy call. Some tests set legacy mock expectations but never assert them, while Delete and DeleteCollection do not set legacy expectations at all, so background mock calls may occur after the test finishes or panic as unexpected calls. These tests do not reliably prove that legacy writes happen.

Mode 3 integration test assumes immediate legacy consistency despite asynchronous writes

The new mode 3 integration test runs the same playlist CRUD suite, which creates/updates/deletes objects through the Kubernetes API and then immediately checks the legacy API. In mode 3, legacy writes are asynchronous, so the legacy API may not yet reflect the change. Without polling/eventual-consistency waits, this test can be flaky and may fail or pass for timing reasons rather than correctness.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

runShardSplitQuery() maps every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables() at line 52, then later executes each shard group through runSplitQuery(). runSplitQuery() was changed to also map every incoming target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables() in querySplitting.ts line 299. As a result, sharded expressions are interpolated again after the __stream_shard__ matcher has been injected. The added test even expects five interpolation calls for one target. Template interpolation is not guaranteed to be idempotent; repeated calls can duplicate ad-hoc filters or reinterpret variable syntax introduced by the first interpolation. Interpolation should be performed in only one layer.

If a raw expression is a template variable that resolves to an empty string, the target passes the non-empty filter, becomes empty after interpolation, and is still grouped and sent to Loki. This can create invalid empty queries. Add a non-empty expr filter after interpolation; the same problem exists in runShardSplitQuery().

A target whose expression is a variable that expands to an empty string will still enter splitQueriesByStreamShard(), potentially causing shard-label lookups for an empty selector and sending an empty query downstream. Targets should be filtered again after applyTemplateVariables().

Because the limit is only enforced for requests that supply this client-controlled header, a client can avoid being counted or blocked simply by omitting the header. When anonStore.DeleteDevice fails, untagDevice logs the outer err variable, which has already been checked to be nil, instead of errD returned by DeleteDevice. The resulting log message does not contain the actual deletion error.

AnonymousDeviceLimit is read with MustInt64(0), and anonstore only enforces the limit when deviceLimit > 0. A negative configuration value therefore disables limiting instead of being rejected or clamped to zero, which can hide operator mistakes.

No tests cover device-limit enforcement and cache interaction

false_positives.candidate:
Translation cache key ignores dynamic fallback chain

The LRU cache key only contains the translation key, current locale, and backend object id. This PR makes fallback resolution depend on SiteSetting.default_locale (and always :en). If two requests use the same I18n.locale but have different default locales (for example in multisite, or after an admin changes default_locale without a full I18n cache clear), a fallback translation cached for one context can be returned for another, serving the wrong language until the cache is cleared or evicted. Include the fallback chain/default locale/site identifier in the cache key, or invalidate this cache when fallback inputs change.

Fallback locales are only ensured loaded for controller requests

I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded! is called only in ApplicationController#set_locale. The translate accelerator lazily loads only the current locale inside I18n.translate, so fallback target locales (site default and :en) are not loaded in mailers, Sidekiq jobs, rake tasks, console, middleware, or any code path that translates without passing through this controller filter. In those contexts, missing translations will not fall back and may return translation-missing strings or raise instead. Fallback locales should be ensured whenever I18n.locale is set or inside the translate path.

translate still assumes @loaded_locales is initialized

The new ensure_loaded! method initializes @loaded_locales, but translate still calls @loaded_locales.include?(config.locale) without initializing it. If any code calls I18n.translate before ensure_loaded!, reload!, or load_locale has run, this will raise NoMethodError on nil. translate should use a memoized/synchronized accessor or initialize @loaded_locales before checking it.

No tests for new fallback/loading behavior

This PR changes global I18n fallback order, lazy locale loading, and request-time loading, but adds no specs covering: missing translations falling back to SiteSetting.default_locale and :en; loading of fallback locales outside controllers; or cache invalidation when default_locale changes. Without tests, regressions in fallback behavior or cache staleness are likely.

Data migration is not reversible

The migration uses raw INSERT/DELETE statements inside a `change` method. Rails cannot automatically reverse these operations, so rolling back the migration will raise an irreversible migration error. Use `up`/`down` or an explicit reversible block.

No uniqueness enforcement for host

The model validates only the format of `host`; there is no uniqueness validation and the migration does not add a unique index. Duplicate host rows can be created, and `record_for_host` uses `.first`, making the selected category nondeterministic when duplicates exist.

category_id is not validated against existing categories

The update action renders the current embedding object but never applies or persists any parameters. The client controller has a saveChanges action that calls `embedding.update({})`; any future editable embedding attributes sent to this endpoint would silently not save.

After saving, the component sets `category` by looking up the local `categoryId`, but does not update `category_id`, and the lookup may return undefined. If the server coerces a blank category to uncategorized or the category cannot be found, the displayed row may show no category or stale state.

The loop makes at most five 80% resize attempts and ignores the boolean returned by OptimizedImage.downsize. If conversion fails or five attempts are insufficient, execution still proceeds to Upload.create_for with a file that may exceed SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb. The controller should verify the final size and return an error if it cannot reduce the file enough, rather than relying on later behavior.

Image processing command is executed via string interpolation without escaping

convert_with runs a shell command built from instructions.join(' ') using backticks. Paths are inserted as unquoted, unescaped arguments. The new automatic downsizing passes temporary file paths to this code; if a path contains spaces or shell metacharacters, the command can fail or execute unintended commands. Use system with an argument array or Shellwords.escape instead of interpolating into a shell string.

The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

If the user has no topic_users row for that topic, tu is nil and the request raises NoMethodError. true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same nil dereference: when no TopicUser record exists, tu is nil and calling a method on it crashes.

State-changing unsubscribe is performed via GET

The /t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe route is a GET route and TopicsController#unsubscribe immediately mutates TopicUser.notification_level. GET requests are not protected by Rails CSRF tokens and can be triggered by link prefetching, email-client previews, or embedded resources while a user is logged in. Repeated GETs also move regular users to muted. Use a POST/PUT action with CSRF protection or require an explicit confirmation before changing state.

The action updates TopicUser with tu.save! instead of TopicUser.change. Make the topic-specific line conditional on unsubscribe_url being present or update all callers.

Topic title is rendered unescaped with triple braces

The template renders {{{stopNotificiationsText}}}, and that property interpolates model.fancyTitle into an HTML string. Triple braces bypass Handlebars escaping, so any HTML in the topic title, or in a future representation of fancyTitle, would be injected into the page. Escape the title or render it through a safe component.

The PR adds a state-changing unsubscribe endpoint and a new required unsubscribe_url interpolation, but the only spec change merely passes unsubscribe_url to Email::MessageBuilder and still only asserts the global preferences URL. There are no controller/request specs for TopicsController#unsubscribe, including missing TopicUser rows, notification-level transitions, slug redirects, or HTML/JSON behavior, and no spec asserting that the topic unsubscribe URL appears in email bodies or HTML.

true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same issue: date formatting hardcodes 'en-US' instead of using the user's active locale from useLocale, causing incorrect locale-specific date representation.

The input schema uses z.number(), which accepts floating-point values, but credential IDs are integer primary keys. Use z.number().int(), and optionally positive, so malformed input is rejected before reaching Prisma.

true_positives.matched_candidate:

checkIfIsAvailable uses workingHours.find and marks the slot unavailable if any working-hours entry reports the slot outside that entry. With multiple working-hour entries on the same day, a slot that is valid in one entry is outside another, so it is incorrectly rejected. true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))

The zero-length override check compares two Day.js objects with ===. This compares object identity and is always false for distinct Day.js instances, even if they represent the same instant. Use .isSame() if start and end equality is intended.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that === compares Day.js object references rather than date values, making the equality check fail for distinct instances, and recommend using .isSame().

checkIfIsAvailable sets dateOverrideExist when it sees any override on the slot's UTC date and, if the slot is not rejected by the override conditions, returns true before the busy.every() check. As a result, any busy periods or accepted bookings for that user are ignored for slots covered by a date override, so users can be offered and potentially book slots that are already busy.

Multiple date overrides for the same day are handled as mutually exclusive

The date override test uses dateOverrides.find and returns false when the slot is outside the iterated override. If a user has two date overrides on the same date, a slot inside the first override is outside the second, so find returns the second override and the slot is rejected. The correct condition is that the slot is inside at least one override, not outside any override.

The code treats a slot as outside an override only if slotEndTime is before or equal to the override start, or slotStartTime is after the override end. Therefore a slot that starts before the override and ends inside it, or starts inside and ends after it, is considered inside the override. The PR description says round-robin slots must respect fixed hosts' date overrides, but the added test only checks a personal event in another timezone. There is no regression test for round-robin with fixed hosts, multiple overrides, or busy times during a date override.

Inside timeSlots.filter, fixedHosts = userAvailability.filter(...) is computed for each slot. Since userAvailability does not change during the loop, this repeats work for every slot; compute fixedHosts once before filtering.

true_positives.reasoning: Both identify lost retryCount increments caused by writing a stale reminder.retryCount + 1 under concurrency, including both failure paths, and recommend Prisma's atomic increment operation.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.

true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same missing SMS method filter in the retryCount > 1 deletion OR branch, which incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders such as Email and WhatsApp.

false_positives.candidate:

In the catch block, the retry-count update is not protected. If the reminder was deleted by another process or the database update fails, this update throws and terminates the handler, preventing the remaining reminders in the batch from being processed. Use updateMany or wrap this update in its own try/catch.

All exceptions count toward the SMS retry limit

The catch block increments retryCount for any exception thrown while preparing the SMS, including transient database errors, metadata validation errors, or template errors. After two such errors the reminder is deleted, even if the SMS provider was never contacted or the failure is transient. Consider counting only SMS provider failures or using a separate failure-handling path for unexpected errors.

When message is empty or sendTo is falsy, the code skips scheduling and does not increment retryCount. true_positives.golden_comment: Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

The only actual database execution in this suite is the simple user-scope query. Placeholder refresh_token can overwrite real refresh token

If a refreshed token response does not include refresh_token, the code sets refresh_token to the literal string "refresh_token". Callers that spread this parsed data into stored credentials, such as Office 365 and Zoom, can overwrite the real refresh token with this placeholder, permanently breaking future OAuth refreshes for that credential.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: a missing refresh_token in an OAuth refresh response is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token", overwriting a valid token and breaking subsequent refreshes.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.

Subsequent credential reads will fail googleCredentialSchema.parse because the stored key is wrapped with success/data instead of containing the raw OAuth credentials.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse wrapper, which is incorrectly persisted as credential.key instead of the parsed OAuth token data.

true_positives.golden_comment: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. Google refresh assumes response.data but sync returns fetch Response

Google refresh assumes response.data but sync returns fetch Response

refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response when credential sync is enabled, but GoogleCalendarService treats the result as a Google API response and accesses res?.data. In sync mode res.data is undefined, so accessing token.access_token throws and Google Calendar token refresh fails.

When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, parseRefreshTokenResponse ignores the app-specific schema for every credential, even when refreshOAuthTokens falls back to the normal refresh path, such as for team credentials. When credential sync is enabled, refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response, but HubspotCalendarService treats the return value as a parsed HubspotToken and reads expiresIn from it. The normal Zoho Bigin refresh path returns an Axios response with a data property, but when credential sync is enabled refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response. The code then reads tokenInfo.data.error and mutates tokenInfo.data, which will throw or corrupt token handling for Zoho Bigin credentials.

The normal Zoho CRM refresh path returns an Axios response with a data property, but when credential sync is enabled refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response. The code then reads zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error and mutates zohoCrmTokenInfo.data, which will throw or corrupt token handling for Zoho CRM credentials.

SalesforceCalendarService calls prisma.credential.update but does not import prisma. This will throw a ReferenceError at runtime whenever Salesforce credential refresh attempts to persist the new access token.

getClient performs an OAuth refresh-token request unconditionally, even if the stored access token is still valid. Because calendar service instances are created during normal event operations, this can generate excessive Salesforce token refresh requests, hit rate limits, and cause token rotation problems.

Unlike the other updated OAuth integrations, Salesforce refreshes directly against login.salesforce.com and never calls refreshOAuthTokens. refreshOAuthTokens returns the raw fetch Response from CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT without checking response.ok or parsing JSON, while callers expect different shapes: some expect a parsed token object, some an Axios response, and some a fetch Response. The webhook handler performs findFirst followed by update or create without a transaction or unique constraint. Concurrent webhook calls for the same user/app can both find no existing credential and create duplicate credentials, leading to unpredictable app behavior and future updates only touching one duplicate.

When updating an existing credential, the webhook only writes key. If the credential was previously marked invalid, for example after an invalid_grant refresh failure, the newly synced valid credential remains marked invalid and may continue to be unusable.

The webhook secret header is compared to CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET using !== instead of a constant-time comparison. For a secret-protected endpoint that can write OAuth credentials, a constant-time comparison is safer against timing-based secret leakage.

This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

false_positives.candidate:

The handler refunds paid bookings and returns before reaching the scheduled-job cancellation and workflow reminder cancellation code later in the function. As a result, cancelled/rejected paid bookings can keep active workflow reminders and scheduled jobs, so reminder emails/SMS may still be sent.

Cancelled-reminder query does not restrict to scheduled email reminders with a batch ID

SpanFlusher.join breaks out of the process cleanup loop when the deadline has expired, so flusher processes are not terminated. If next_step.join(timeout) consumes the whole timeout, or the deadline expires while waiting for one process, remaining background flushers keep running after join returns. Because they continue to poll Redis and produce to Kafka, a rebalance or restart can leak processes and duplicate segments. Terminate all processes even after timeout, and preferably join them after termination.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same problem: when the deadline expires, breaking out of the loop skips terminating the remaining flusher processes, so they keep running after shutdown. Both also propose the same fix, which is to always attempt termination.

false_positives.candidate:
Unhealthy flusher worker is replaced without ensuring it has stopped

In _ensure_processes_alive, an unhealthy worker is killed only if it is a multiprocessing.Process, and the code does not wait for it to exit before creating a replacement. For threading.Thread workers, used when produce_to_pipe is set, there is no way to stop the old thread at all. The old worker can therefore continue flushing the same shards while the replacement runs, causing duplicate Kafka production or conflicting Redis updates. Ensure the old worker has terminated, or fence it, before starting a new one.

Health timestamp is not updated during long flush or produce cycles

SpanFlusher.main updates healthy_since once per loop before producing and waiting for Kafka futures. If flush_segments, produce, or future.result takes longer than spans.buffer.flusher.max-unhealthy-seconds, submit/_ensure_processes_alive will classify the process as hung and kill/restart it mid-flush. That can duplicate partially produced segments. Update the heartbeat during long flush/produce operations or include produce wait time in health reporting.

--flusher-processes accepts non-positive values

The new --flusher-processes option is an unbounded int. A negative value is passed to SpanFlusher, where num_processes can become negative; with assigned shards the subsequent process/shard mapping can fail with a confusing KeyError instead of a clear CLI validation error. Use click.IntRange(min=1) or validate the value in the factory/flusher.

Docstring says one process per shard, but processes are capped and shared

The SpanFlusher docstring says it creates one process per shard, but the implementation creates min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards)) processes and assigns multiple shards to the same process when max_processes is smaller. The CLI default is 1, so the actual behavior is not one process per shard. Update the docstring and help text to describe the actual process-sharing behavior.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

In BaseDetectorTypeValidator.update(), the code does `validated_data.get("detector_type", instance.group_type)`. This means the `.get("detector_type", ...)` always falls back to `instance.group_type`, making it impossible to update the detector type via PUT. The key should be `"type"` to match the serializer field name.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
zip(error_ids, events.values()) misaligns when nodestore returns fewer results

In fetch_error_details, `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` returns a dict that may omit keys for missing events. The code then does `zip(error_ids, events.values())`, which pairs error_ids positionally with whatever values the dict contains. If any event_id is not found in nodestore, the dict will have fewer entries than error_ids, causing subsequent event_ids to be paired with the wrong event data. For example, with error_ids=[a,b,c] and only a,c found, the zip produces (a,data_a) and (b,data_c), attributing c's data to b. The fix is to iterate over node_ids and look up each in the returned dict, e.g. `for node_id, event_id in zip(node_ids, error_ids): data = events.get(node_id)`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same code: zip(error_ids, events.values()) misaligning event data with IDs. The golden comment names two causes, order not being preserved and missing nodes shifting alignment. The candidate focuses on the missing-nodes cause and proposes a fix by key lookup, which also resolves the ordering concern. Same underlying bug.

Falsy check on age/timestamp allows both fields when age=0

If a report contains both `"age": 0` and `"timestamp": 123`, the `self.initial_data.get("age")` check returns 0 (falsy), so the mutual-exclusion validation is silently skipped and both fields are accepted. The check should use `"age" in self.initial_data` or `self.initial_data.get("age") is not None` instead.

The candidate focuses on age=0 and the golden mentions the timestamp check, but both point to the same flawed pattern and suggest the same fix, an `in` check.

false_positives.candidate:
Java MessageFormat syntax introduced into an i18next message bundle

The account-ui message bundle uses i18next/react-i18next placeholders elsewhere, such as '{{app}}' and '{{date}}'. The changed 'error-invalid-multivalued-size' message now uses '{0}', '{1}', and '{2,choice,...}', which i18next will not interpolate or evaluate as Java MessageFormat. As a result, the account UI will show the raw pattern or a broken validation message when this error occurs. This key should keep i18next-compatible interpolation/pluralization or the UI localization layer needs explicit support for this format.

Java MessageFormat syntax introduced into an i18next message bundle

The admin-ui message bundle is used with i18next-style interpolation, and this key previously used '{{0}}', '{{1}}', and '{{2}}'. It was changed to '{0}', '{1}', and '{2,choice,...}', which is Java MessageFormat syntax and is not understood by i18next. The admin UI will therefore not substitute the parameters or pluralize the message correctly. This is a user-visible localization/contract break for the admin UI.

Property resource bundles are read without explicit UTF-8 decoding

verifySafeHtml() constructs PropertyResourceBundle directly from a FileInputStream. That path uses the legacy Properties InputStream loading behavior, which is not appropriate for the UTF-8 theme message files used by Keycloak (Arabic, Chinese, Cyrillic, etc.). Non-ASCII values can be garbled before HTML verification, leading to incorrect validation results or spurious failures. Use an InputStreamReader with StandardCharsets.UTF_8 when creating the PropertyResourceBundle.

Choice expressions are stripped before sanitization, hiding any markup they contain

normalizeValue() replaces the entire '{n,choice,...}' expression with '...' for linkExpirationFormatter.timePeriodUnit* keys and error-invalid-multivalued-size. Any HTML placed inside the choice alternatives is therefore never passed to the OWASP sanitizer. Since these messages can be rendered in HTML themes or emails, markup can bypass the check by being embedded in a choice expression. The verifier should validate the textual choice alternatives instead of discarding the whole expression.

English companion file path is derived with fragile replaceAll regexes

The English file path is computed by applying replaceAll('resources-community', 'resources') and replaceAll('_[a-zA-Z-_]*\.properties', '_en.properties') to the absolute path. This operates on the whole path rather than the file name, so matching substrings outside the message file name can produce a wrong path. It can also fail for locale suffixes not matched by the regex. If the derived path is wrong, verification fails with an inability-to-read-file error. Resolve the English companion from the file name and locale instead of regex-replacing the absolute path.

templateHelp normalization removes arbitrary uppercase tags after CLAIM.

The normalization for templateHelp removes any uppercase tag following 'CLAIM.' rather than only the intended literal text 'CLAIM.<NAME>'. This hides markup such as 'CLAIM.<B>' or 'CLAIM.<SCRIPT>' from the sanitizer. If this help text is ever rendered as HTML, the verifier could pass unsafe markup. Use an exact quoted replacement for 'CLAIM.<NAME>' or a precise allow-list.

Danish email HTML still contains a stray 'n' before 'Hvis' identityProviderLinkBodyHtml was fixed to close the final paragraph, but the text still reads '

nHvis du ikke vil forbinde disse konti...'. The leading 'n' appears to be a typo or leftover and will be shown to users. It should be '

Hvis du ikke vil forbinde disse konti...'.

Test resource loading uses URL.getFile() without URL decoding

getFile() creates a File from resource.getFile(). URL.getFile() does not decode URL-encoded characters such as '%20', so tests can fail when the repository path contains spaces or other characters that are percent-encoded. Use Paths.get(resource.toURI()).toFile() instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.

true_positives.golden_comment: Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
testIncorrectGrantType succeeds due to NullPointerException from uninitialized sessionFactory

The test creates DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory without calling postInit, so sessionFactory is null. When getTokenContextFromTokenId sees the unknown shortcut 'ac', it attempts to refresh grant mappings and throws NullPointerException, which is caught as RuntimeException. The test therefore does not verify the intended invalid-grant-shortcut behavior; it should initialize or mock the factory and assert the specific IllegalArgumentException.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point out that the test catches a generic RuntimeException when it should assert the specific IllegalArgumentException. The candidate adds a root cause (an NPE from the uninitialized sessionFactory), but it explicitly recommends asserting IllegalArgumentException, so it covers the same concern.

false_positives.candidate:
Grant shortcuts are accepted without null or length validation

DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit stores OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut() directly without checking that it is non-null and exactly two characters long. The default encoder/decoder hard-codes a six-character context prefix composed of three two-character shortcuts. A null shortcut will cause a NullPointerException when inserted into ConcurrentHashMap, and a one- or three-character shortcut will produce token IDs whose prefix cannot be parsed by getTokenContextFromTokenId, which expects length 6. Shortcut format should be validated when factories are registered.

New abstract getShortcut method breaks existing OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementations

Adding String getShortcut() to OAuth2GrantTypeFactory without a default implementation is a source and binary compatibility break for custom grant type factories compiled against earlier Keycloak versions. Existing implementations will fail to compile or can fail at runtime when the token-context encoder invokes the missing method. If this SPI is expected to be implemented by extensions, a default method or explicit migration contract is needed.

Copy constructor removed from OAuth2GrantType.Context

The change removes the public copy constructor OAuth2GrantType.Context(Context). If custom grant implementations or downstream code used this constructor, they will break at compile time or runtime with NoSuchMethodError. The addition of the grantType field could have preserved the copy constructor, or the removal should be explicitly documented as an incompatible SPI change.

Dynamic grant shortcut refresh is non-atomic and does not enforce uniqueness

getShortcutByGrantType and getGrantTypeByShortcut lazily add mappings for newly deployed grant types by writing to two separate ConcurrentHashMap instances without synchronization or duplicate-shortcut validation. If a newly deployed grant uses a shortcut already used by another grant, it can overwrite the existing shortcut-to-grant mapping, causing previously issued token IDs to decode to the wrong grant type. Concurrent updates can also observe partially updated state between the two maps. The maps should be updated atomically and uniqueness should be rechecked before insertion.

setFormParams does not update cached grantType

OAuth2GrantType.Context.grantType is derived from formParams.getFirst(OAuth2Constants.GRANT_TYPE) only in the constructor. setFormParams replaces the form parameters but leaves grantType unchanged, so getGrantType() can return a stale value if the form parameters are modified after construction. The setter should update grantType or getGrantType should compute it from the current formParams.

If a federated user already has a local recovery-code credential, for example created earlier as a fallback, that credential remains in the local store and can still be validated. true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. true_positives.matched_candidate:

In GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission(), the code evaluates and stores groupResource.getId(). For V2 group resources, the actual group ID is the resource name, not the authorization resource ID. The returned set is later used as group IDs for user search/count filtering (UserModel.GROUPS), so filtering is done with internal authorization IDs, and may also include the 'Groups' type resource. AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource() creates individual resources for groups, users, and clients with resourceStore.create(...) and updates their scopes, but it never calls resource.setType(resourceType). GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() later looks up group resources with resourceStore.findByType(server, GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...). Because individual group resources have no type, that query only finds the type-level 'Groups' resource and misses all per-group resources, breaking group-restricted user queries and counts.

AdminPermissions.registerListener() registers a GroupRemovedEvent listener that calls management(...).groups().setPermissionsEnabled(group, false). When V2 admin permissions are enabled, management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2 and GroupPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled() throws UnsupportedOperationException. Depending on feature configuration, this can either make group deletion fail with an exception or leave V2 authorization resources orphaned. The listener needs V2-aware cleanup or a safe no-op.

GroupResource.getManagementPermissions() calls permissions.groups().isPermissionsEnabled(group), and the corresponding PUT endpoint calls setPermissionsEnabled(). GroupPermissionsV2 implements these methods by throwing UnsupportedOperationException. If the V2 feature is active and the V1 feature gate allows the endpoint, requests to /groups/{id}/management/permissions will fail with HTTP 500 instead of returning a safe disabled state or a proper unsupported response.

Impersonation evaluation uses the target user's identity when a requester client is provided

UserPermissionsV2.canImpersonate(UserModel user, ClientModel requester) builds a DefaultEvaluationContext with UserModelIdentity(root.realm, user), i.e. the identity of the user being impersonated, and then evaluates the IMPERSONATE scope. This means the caller/requester identity is not used for the permission evaluation when a requester client is present. Policies granting the calling client or admin the right to impersonate may not match, while policies tied to the target user may control the result. canClientImpersonate() delegates to this method, so client-initiated impersonation authorization is likely incorrect.

Group count endpoint ignores fine-grained group permissions

GroupsResource.getGroupCount() only calls requireList() and then returns realm-wide group counts via getGroupsCountByNameContaining() or getGroupsCount(). Because canList() can be true through QUERY_GROUPS while GET /groups is filtered by canView(group), a caller who cannot view any groups can still learn the total number of groups and the number of groups matching a search string. The count should be filtered using the same permissions as the group listing.

AdminPermissionsSchema.getScope() calls SCHEMA.getResourceTypes().get(resourceType).getScopes() without checking whether resourceType is null or present in the map. A request creating or updating a scope permission with a missing/invalid resource type can therefore cause a NullPointerException and HTTP 500 instead of a validation error.

GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission() falls back to AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(...) when a specific group resource is not found, then immediately calls policyStore.findByResource(server, resource). getResourceTypeResource() can return null if the schema is not supported or the type resource was not initialized, leading to a NullPointerException. The same pattern exists in UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission().

GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() iterates over all Group resources and performs a full policy evaluation for each one. This method is invoked by user search/count endpoints such as UsersResource and BruteForceUsersResource whenever the caller lacks global user view permission. In realms with many groups, every restricted user search can trigger O(number of groups) authorization evaluations, which may be very slow.

Group resource names are not resolved for display

AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceName() only resolves resource names for the Users resource type. For Groups resources it returns resource.getDisplayName(), but individual group resources are created with the group ID as the name and no display name. As a result, authorization policy UIs or representations may show an empty or meaningless identifier instead of the group name/path. A GROUPS case should resolve the group and return a useful name.

true_positives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

ASN1Decoder.readLength returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding, but readInteger passes that value directly to read(int), which allocates new byte[length]. Malformed DER input with an indefinite length therefore causes NegativeArraySizeException instead of a controlled IOException. readSequence also treats a -1 length as an empty sequence rather than rejecting it. The decoder should explicitly reject indefinite and negative lengths.
