The golden comment flags the 'length = length - bytes.length' arithmetic in sequence processing. The candidate mentions readSequence mishandling -1 and readInteger allocating a negative array. These are the same underlying bug, though the candidate emphasizes a different symptom.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract order() method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

CryptoProvider is a public extension point. Adding int order() without a default method breaks source and binary compatibility for external implementations. At runtime CryptoIntegration.detectProvider sorts providers with Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order), so an older implementation that does not have this method will cause AbstractMethodError. A default method should be added to preserve compatibility.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same problem: adding an abstract order() method to the CryptoProvider interface breaks backward compatibility for existing implementations. The candidate adds detail about the runtime AbstractMethodError, but the underlying issue is identical.

false_positives.candidate:
Provider selection is nondeterministic when order values tie

detectProvider sorts providers only by order() in descending order. DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider and WildFlyElytronProvider all return 200. If multiple providers with the same highest order are present on the classpath, the selected provider depends on ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order. Since the previous fail-fast behavior for multiple providers was removed, a misconfigured classpath may silently select an unintended provider. A deterministic tie-breaker or an error on equal highest order would be safer.

ECDSA raw-to-DER conversion does not validate signature length

concatenatedRSToASN1DER computes len = signLength / 2 and copies len bytes from offset 0 and len bytes from offset len without checking that signature.length == signLength, that signLength is positive, or that it is even. If the supplied signature is shorter than expected, System.arraycopy throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException; if it is longer, trailing bytes are silently ignored. Malformed input should be rejected with IOException or IllegalArgumentException.

integerToBytes silently truncates oversized or malformed integers

In asn1derToConcatenatedRS, integerToBytes copies the last qLength bytes whenever BigInteger.toByteArray() is longer than qLength. This is only correct when the extra byte is a leading zero sign byte for a positive integer. The method does not check that the BigInteger is positive, that the value fits in qLength, or that discarded bytes are zero. A malformed or oversized DER integer can therefore be silently converted into an incorrect fixed-length R/S coordinate instead of being rejected.

readSequence does not enforce the declared SEQUENCE length

readSequence subtracts each parsed child TLV length from the declared sequence length and stops when the remaining length is no longer positive. If a child TLV is longer than the remaining declared length, the remaining length becomes negative and parsing stops without error. This accepts malformed DER instead of rejecting it. The parser should throw when the remaining length becomes negative or when the declared content is not consumed exactly.

ECDSA conversion test only checks self-roundtrip, not standard DER validity

The test converts a Java-produced DER signature to concatenated R/S and back, then asserts that the two concatenated arrays are equal. It does not verify that the regenerated DER signature is accepted by java.security.Signature.verify, and it uses a default EC key pair rather than curve-specific keys for ES384/ES512. A self-consistent but non-standard DER encoding could pass this test while failing interoperability. The test should verify the regenerated DER with the public key and/or use known test vectors for each curve.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Concurrent test does not wait for the reader thread and can pass vacuously or hang

The test starts a non-daemon reader thread, deletes the groups, sets deletedAll, and immediately asserts that caughtExceptions is empty. It never joins the thread or waits for at least one read to occur during deletion, so the assertion can run before the reader performs any request or after it has already stopped, missing the race the test is meant to catch. If a delete call throws before deletedAll.set(true), the reader loop may also run indefinitely. Use a latch/join, ensure reads overlap with deletes, and stop the thread in a finally block.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same flaw: the test never joins or waits for the reader thread. The golden comment says asserting right after setting deletedAll can race and miss exceptions. The candidate says the assertion can run before the reader performs any request or after it has stopped, which is the same race.

true_positives.golden_comment: In UsernameForm.authenticate(), isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() is called without passing the required UserModel parameter.

Call to undefined isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.

In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features is true and cursor.offset < 0, start_offset is set to the negative offset and queryset[start_offset:stop] is evaluated. Django QuerySet slicing does not support negative start/stop values and raises AssertionError. Because cursor offsets are parsed from client-supplied strings, this allows a request to trigger a 500 instead of paginating.

The golden comment ties it to organization_auditlogs.py and the candidate ties it to get_result, but it is the same paginator and the same problem.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.

OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint.get passes order_by='-datetime' with OptimizedCursorPaginator. When any audit-log rows are returned, the key function receives a datetime and raises TypeError, and any non-empty cursor value would be compared as an integer to a datetime column. true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BuildIndex can run concurrently for the same namespaced resource

The patch removes the global lock around BuildIndex but adds no per-key synchronization or singleflight. GetIndex returns nil until BuildIndex inserts the finished index, so concurrent Search or watch-event calls for the same namespace/group/resource can both start builds. This duplicates work, can open the same file-backed bleve directory concurrently, and lets the last writer replace another live index in the cache without closing it. Add a per-key lock or reserve the key while building.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same problem. Removing the lock around BuildIndex lets concurrent goroutines build the same key's index at once, which duplicates expensive work.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the index cache without locking

bleveBackend.TotalDocs ranges over b.cache while BuildIndex may concurrently write to that map. TotalDocs does not take cacheMu.RLock, so this is an unsynchronized map read/write that can panic or return wrong totals. This is more likely now that BuildIndex only locks for the cache insertion.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: TotalDocs iterates b.cache with no lock while BuildIndex writes to the map concurrently, which can cause a concurrent map read/write panic. The candidate does not mention the watcher goroutine as the trigger, but the underlying problem is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
Unsynchronized shared writes in search init workers

searchSupport.init starts multiple errgroup workers that all increment totalBatchesIndexed and assign to the outer err variable. These are shared variables with no mutex, atomic, or local handling, so concurrent index builds race. The reported indexed count can be wrong, an error can be overwritten, and the Go race detector will fail.

History and Origin dereference s.search without nil checks

server.History calls s.search.History and server.Origin calls s.search.Origin, but s.search can be nil when search is not configured. server.Search checks for this case, while History and Origin will panic on a nil pointer if invoked. Add nil checks or return a not-configured error.

Watch loop does not handle closed event channel

The goroutine started in searchSupport.init receives from events with v := <-events and passes v to handleEvent. If the storage backend closes the channel, the receive returns a nil *WrittenEvent repeatedly, and handleEvent dereferences evt.Type, causing a panic. The loop also has no context.Done branch, so it cannot be stopped cleanly. Use v, ok := <-events and stop when !ok, and select on a cancellable context.

IndexMetrics is used without nil checks in handleEvent

handleEvent increments and decrements IndexMetrics.IndexedKinds for added and deleted events without checking whether IndexMetrics is nil. Other parts of the code guard with if IndexMetrics != nil. If metrics are not initialized, any ADDED or DELETED watch event will panic.

BuildIndex uses IndexMetrics without nil check

BuildIndex increments resource.IndexMetrics.IndexTenants unconditionally. Since other code paths check whether IndexMetrics is nil, this can panic when metrics are disabled or uninitialized. Guard the metric calls or guarantee initialization.

Constructor leaks context/lifecycle resources when Init fails

NewResourceServer creates a cancellable context and may run lifecycle initialization before s.Init. If s.Init returns an error, the constructor returns without calling cancel or stopping lifecycle hooks, leaking the context and any initialized backend resources. Clean up on the error path.

Initial index build can miss events written before the watch starts

searchSupport.init builds all indexes first and only then calls WatchWriteEvents. Writes that happen while the initial build is running are not included in the built index and are not replayed by the watcher, which starts after the build. In deployments with concurrent writers or other instances, the search index can remain stale until affected resources are written again.

Postgres storage-server integration test is skipped

The test now skips for GRAFANA_TEST_DB=postgres, so the storage server startup path is not exercised against Postgres in CI. Since this PR changes initialization timing and index building, this reduces coverage for a supported database; the skip should be tied to a tracked fix rather than left as an indefinite TODO.

MetricAlertDetectorHandler subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler but does not implement the abstract members counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and build_occurrence_and_event_data. Any attempt to get the handler for a metric_alert_fire detector will raise TypeError instead of evaluating or safely no-oping. true_positives.golden_comment: Docstring says this returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult, but the method now returns a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey. Consider updating the docstring to match the new return type.

true_positives.reasoning: Both comments make the same point: the docstring says the method returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult, but it actually returns a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey.

false_positives.candidate:
get_state_data raises KeyError when counter_names is empty

In StatefulDetectorHandler.get_state_data, counter_updates is initialized to {} and only populated if self.counter_names is truthy. Later DetectorStateData is constructed with counter_updates[gk] for every group key. If a subclass legitimately has counter_names == [], this raises KeyError for the first group key, making such a stateful detector unusable. Use a default mapping such as counter_updates.get(gk, {}) or always populate defaults for every requested group key.

Dedupe marker is advanced before validating condition group

evaluate_group_key_value calls enqueue_dedupe_update(group_key, dedupe_value) before checking self.condition_group. process_detectors later calls commit_state_updates even when evaluate returns no results, so a packet that was skipped because the detector has no condition group still persists the new dedupe value. If the missing condition group is temporary or corrected later, that packet will never be re-evaluated, potentially losing alert transitions. The dedupe update should probably only be committed after the packet has actually been evaluated, or at least not when skipping for invalid configuration.

Occurrences are emitted before state updates are committed

process_detectors calls create_issue_occurrence_from_result for every result and only afterwards calls handler.commit_state_updates(). If producing one of the occurrences or the subsequent state commit fails, the dedupe/state changes are not persisted. On retry the same packet will be evaluated again, and any occurrences already produced before the failure can be emitted again. Since this PR makes detector handlers produce real IssueOccurrence/StatusChangeMessage payloads, this path can create duplicate issues unless occurrence identifiers are guaranteed idempotent.

get_group_key_values type annotation excludes supported None group key

The abstract signature should be dict[DetectorGroupKey, int], or otherwise document None as a valid key, so subclasses and type checkers match the runtime behavior.

In TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe, the test evaluates evaluate_group_key_value with group_key 'group_key', but the expected occurrence is built with build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, 'val1', ...), giving it a fingerprint for 'val1'. If IssueOccurrence equality includes fingerprint, this test will fail; if equality ignores fingerprint, the test does not verify that the produced occurrence corresponds to the evaluated group key. The expected occurrence should be built with the same group_key being evaluated.

true_positives.golden_comment: The function modifies the config variable to include display values but then returns the original monitor.config instead of the modified version.

Modified monitor config copy is discarded when building event context

get_monitor_environment_context copies the monitor config and replaces schedule_type in the local config variable with the human-readable display value, but the returned dictionary uses monitor_environment.monitor.config instead of the modified local config. As a result, the prepared schedule_type display value is discarded and the emitted monitor context still contains the raw config value. The returned dict should use the modified config variable.

false_positives.candidate:
Failure threshold can be triggered without enough failed check-ins

In try_incident_threshold, when failure_issue_threshold is greater than 1, the code slices the latest check-ins to at most the threshold but never verifies that it actually obtained failure_issue_threshold check-ins. If a monitor with threshold 3 has only one failed check-in, previous_checkins will contain one failure, the OK-check will pass, and the code will set the environment to ERROR and create a MonitorIncident. This creates incidents and issue occurrences before the configured failure threshold is reached. A length check such as returning False when len(previous_checkins) < failure_issue_threshold is needed before changing status or creating the incident.

Previous check-in selection is nondeterministic when timestamps tie

The query that selects previous check-ins orders only by -date_added. If multiple check-ins have identical date_added values, the subset chosen at the threshold boundary and the selected starting_checkin can be nondeterministic. Adding a tie-breaker such as -id would make the threshold evaluation stable.

Occurrences may be created in arbitrary order for threshold check-ins

previous_checkins is explicitly reversed into oldest-to-newest order, but the later queryset uses filter(id__in=...) without an order_by. The resulting MonitorCheckIn rows may be returned in arbitrary order, so create_incident_occurrence can be invoked in a different order than the check-ins being represented. true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.

The dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now(). Python evaluates this default when the class is defined, so every AssignmentSource created without an explicit queued value receives the same import-time datetime instead of the current time. This makes the field misleading for debugging and incorrect for any future logic that relies on it. Use field(default_factory=timezone.now).

true_positives.golden_comment: to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

Task kwargs are serialized across process boundaries; if the Celery serializer is JSON or another non-pickle serializer, this can raise TypeError and prevent the sync task from being enqueued. Even if it serializes to a string, AssignmentSource.from_dict does not parse it back into a datetime. Serialize queued to an ISO string, omit it, or explicitly handle conversion in from_dict.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. to_dict leaves queued as a datetime, the dict is passed into Celery task kwargs, and a JSON serializer can fail on it, which causes enqueue errors.

false_positives.candidate:

AssignmentSource.from_dict catches TypeError and ValueError and returns None. The outbound cycle-prevention logic treats None as no source, so a malformed or partially serialized payload can cause outbound sync to run and potentially recreate the sync loop this PR is trying to prevent. At minimum, log or metric this failure; consider stricter validation or safer fallback behavior.

should_sync returns False whenever sync_source.integration_id matches the installation's integration, regardless of which external issue triggered the inbound change. If a Sentry group is linked to multiple external issues belonging to the same integration, an inbound assignment change from one issue suppresses outbound assignment updates to all other linked issues in that integration. This can leave linked external issues inconsistent. If the intent is only to avoid echoing back to the originating issue, AssignmentSource should also carry the external issue key and the check should be per issue.

The Celery task sync_assignee_outbound now accepts assignment_source_dict, and producers immediately include it in apply_async kwargs. During a rolling deploy, a worker running the previous task signature will receive an unexpected keyword argument and fail with TypeError, causing sync tasks to error or retry. If task producers and workers can be deployed independently, additive task signature changes need compatibility handling or deploy-order guarantees.

The added tests cover assignment with a matching AssignmentSource, but there is no test that GroupAssignee.objects.deassign(..., assignment_source=AssignmentSource.from_integration(integration)) suppresses outbound sync to the same integration. Since the PR changes the deassign path as well, this path should also be covered.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.

false_positives.candidate:
Strategy shuts down the shared FixedQueuePool, breaking later strategy instances

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), but the pool is created by ResultsStrategyFactory and is shared across strategies. Arroyo may close a strategy during a rebalance and then create a new strategy from the same factory. Once close() has shut down the shared pool, worker threads are stopped and queues are closed, so the next strategy will submit to a dead pool. Its submit() exception handler can then mark offsets complete without processing. This can silently drop messages after any rebalance. The strategy should not shut down a factory-owned pool, or a new pool should be created per strategy.

join() ignores its timeout and does not drain queued work before stopping commits

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join() simply calls close(), ignoring the timeout argument. close() stops the commit thread before queue_pool.shutdown() drains remaining queued items, and it never waits for queues or outstanding offsets to become empty. As a result, work processed during shutdown may never have its offsets committed, and shutdown can still block for fixed internal timeouts rather than respecting the requested join timeout.

Shutdown flag can cause queued work items to be dropped

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown = True before allowing queues to drain. OrderedQueueWorker.run() loops on while not self.shutdown, so if a worker is processing an item when shutdown begins it will exit after that one item even if its queue still contains pending work. Although q.shutdown(immediate=False) is intended to permit graceful draining, the worker flag prevents that and can discard queued messages without processing or committing them.

Failed work items are marked complete and become eligible for commit

OrderedQueueWorker.run() catches exceptions from the result processor and still calls offset_tracker.complete_offset() in the finally block. ResultProcessor.__call__ also swallows exceptions. Therefore a result that fails processing is treated as completed and can be committed, despite the strategy documentation saying offsets are committed only after successful processing. A transient failure, such as a database or downstream outage, can permanently lose results with no retry or DLQ.

OffsetTracker iterates shared partition dictionary while other threads may add partitions

OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets() iterates list(self.all_offsets.keys()) without a global lock, while add_offset() may concurrently create new partition entries in self.all_offsets from the submit thread. This can cause dictionary-changed-size-during-iteration errors or missed partitions in the commit loop. Per-partition locks protect individual offset sets but do not protect the partition key collection itself.

Unbounded queues provide no backpressure despite documented guarantee

FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() instances with no maxsize and submit() puts work unconditionally. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.poll() only emits metrics and never applies backpressure. The class documentation claims natural backpressure when queues fill up, but unbounded queues never fill. If workers are slower than the consumer, messages and full Kafka payloads will accumulate in memory without bound and can OOM the process.

FilteredPayload is handled through the generic exception path

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() passes FilteredPayload messages to the decoder. When used with ResultsStrategyFactory.decode_payload(), that decoder asserts the payload is not FilteredPayload, causing an AssertionError that is caught by the generic except branch and logged as 'Error submitting message to queue'. This turns normal filtered messages into exception log spam and relies on exception handling for control flow. FilteredPayload should be explicitly treated as a skipped/completed offset before decoding.

Error-handling test is flaky and asserts behavior opposite to the implementation

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling mocks the result processor to raise for the first message and then asserts that no offsets were committed. However, the worker catches processing exceptions and marks the failed offset complete, so once the commit loop ticks the implementation will commit past the failed message. The test only waits briefly and may pass or fail depending on whether the 1-second commit loop runs before the assertion. It does not reliably validate the intended behavior and masks the fact that failed items are committed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.
The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

When enable_advanced_features is true and cursor.offset is negative, OptimizedCursorPaginator slices the queryset with a negative start offset. Django ORM querysets do not support negative slicing, and the computed stop offset may also be negative or nonsensical. The comment stating that the ORM handles boundary conditions is incorrect; this will cause exceptions or undefined pagination behavior.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same issue: in OptimizedCursorPaginator, when advanced features are enabled and the cursor offset is negative, that offset is used directly as the start of the queryset slice. That is invalid for a Django queryset.

true_positives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.

A crafted cursor such as 0:-10:1 can cause an AssertionError or database error and result in a 500 response on any endpoint using BasePaginator or DateTimePaginator.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug: BasePaginator.get_result uses an unclamped negative offset when cursor.is_prev is true, and that offset reaches queryset slicing.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key calls math.floor/math.ceil directly on the ordered field value, and value_from_cursor returns the raw cursor value. In organization_auditlogs.py it is used with order_by='-datetime'. For any non-empty result page, math.ceil(datetime) raises TypeError, and for non-zero cursors the WHERE clause would compare a datetime column to a numeric value. The optimized audit-log pagination path is therefore broken.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same problem as the golden comment. It names get_item_key, which calls math.floor/ceil on a datetime ordered field with order_by='-datetime', and says this raises a TypeError.

true_positives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unguarded access to organization_context.member may raise AttributeError

The code accesses organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking whether organization_context.member is None. If a request has an organization context without a member, this will raise AttributeError and return a 500 instead of denying access or falling back safely.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same unguarded access chain, organization_context.member.has_global_access, raising AttributeError for users who are not members. The golden comment says organization_context is None, while the candidate says member is None. That is a small difference, but it is the same bug at the same location for the same user case.

false_positives.candidate:
New optimized pagination path is untested

The PR adds a new optimized_pagination query-parameter branch and uses OptimizedCursorPaginator, but no tests cover this endpoint behavior or the new paginator. Given the datetime incompatibility and negative-offset handling, this is a high-risk untested code path.

Switch from Redis sets to sorted sets is not backward compatible with in-flight data

Existing span-buf:s:* keys created by the previous code are Redis sets. The new code uses ZADD here, and the Lua script uses ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE, while flushing uses ZSCAN. During a rollout, pre-existing set-typed keys will cause WRONGTYPE errors, causing span buffering or flushing to fail until those keys expire. This needs a migration strategy, dual-type handling, or a new key namespace.

ZUNIONSTORE default SUM aggregation can corrupt span scores

ZUNIONSTORE defaults to AGGREGATE SUM. If the same span payload exists in both the destination and source sorted sets, for example due to duplicate delivery, retries, or overlapping buffer keys, its score becomes the sum of end_timestamp_precise values rather than the original timestamp. This corrupts eviction ordering. The union should use an explicit aggregation such as MAX or MIN.

Eviction can silently drop spans, including root spans, while preserving has-root state

The script evicts the lowest-scored members with ZPOPMIN when a segment exceeds 1000 spans. There is no metric or explicit signal that data was dropped. If the evicted member is the root span, the has_root_span key may still be set because is_root_span was observed, causing the segment to be flushed with root-based timing while missing its root span. This can produce incomplete or inconsistent trace segments.

Reduced redirect-following limit may fragment deep traces

The redirect traversal loop was reduced from 10000 to 1000. If a trace has a redirect chain longer than 1000, new spans will stop at an intermediate redirect target and be stored under the wrong set key, fragmenting the segment. The PR provides no migration or test coverage for this behavioral change.

Consumer hard-fails if end_timestamp_precise is missing

The consumer now reads val['end_timestamp_precise'] directly. If an incoming span message omits this field or provides null due to schema drift, older producers, or malformed data, the consumer will raise KeyError or later fail when using the value as a Redis score. This makes the consumer fragile to upstream variations.

No tests cover the new eviction behavior or sorted-set migration

The core behavioral changes in this PR are the switch from sets to sorted sets and eviction of segments above 1000 spans, but the tests only add end_timestamp_precise values. There is no coverage for segments exceeding the span cap, eviction order, root-span eviction, stale queue entries, or compatibility with old set-typed Redis keys.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache key uses Python hash() of project IDs

The cache key embeds `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))`. Python hash values are not a stable, collision-resistant way to build cache keys across processes/versions, and different project sets could collide. Use a deterministic key such as sorted project IDs joined together.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same problem: the cache key is built with Python's built-in hash(), which is not stable across processes. Both recommend serializing the project IDs deterministically instead. The candidate's extra point about collisions does not change that it targets the same issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling decision uses request dataset instead of executed dataset

`_get_event_stats` receives `scoped_dataset` but determines upsampling using the outer `dataset` captured from the request. When the factory substitutes a split dataset (for example dashboard widget split queries), the eligibility check can be based on the wrong dataset, causing the transform to be applied or skipped incorrectly.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. The upsampling eligibility check uses the outer request dataset instead of scoped_dataset, so the decision can be wrong when dashboard split queries swap in a different dataset.

false_positives.candidate:
Accidental submodule/gitlink added

The PR adds a gitlink/submodule (`Subproject commit ...`) at repository root. This is unrelated to the feature and can break checkouts/builds or accidentally vendor another repository. It should be removed.

Eligibility cache has no effective invalidation

`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` caches allowlist eligibility for 60 seconds, but nothing invalidates these keys when `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` changes. The unused `invalidate_upsampling_cache` helper also only deletes one exact project-set key. If the allowlist changes, API responses can return upsampled or non-upsampled counts incorrectly for up to a minute.

`_is_error_focused_query` treats any occurrence of `event.type:error` in the raw query as an error-only query. This matches negated filters like `!event.type:error`, OR clauses that also include transactions, and text/tag values. For discover queries this can replace `count()` with `upsampled_count()` when non-error events are included, producing wrong counts.

upsampled_count is exposed as a public aggregate

The new `upsampled_count` SnQL function is not marked `private=True`, unlike neighboring internal functions. API callers may be able to request it directly, bypassing the allowlist/eligibility logic that only rewrites `count()`, and get incorrect results on projects or datasets where sample weights should not be used.

upsampled_count does not handle missing sample_weight

`upsampled_count` is implemented as `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. If any queried event has NULL/missing `sample_weight` (for example historical events before upsampling was enabled, malformed events, or non-error rows accidentally included in discover), the aggregation can ignore those rows or return NULL/zero, silently changing counts. A fallback or explicit row filtering is needed.

Upsampling can be enabled for errors dataset without function registration

`_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns true for the errors dataset, but the PR only registers `upsampled_count` in the discover dataset converter. If the errors dataset does not inherit that converter, allowlisted requests using `dataset=errors` will generate queries referencing an unknown function and fail.

Top-events path only transforms timeseries columns

For `topEvents > 0`, the PR transforms `timeseries_columns`/`y_axes` but leaves `selected_columns`, `equations`, and `orderby` untransformed. If those fields contain or depend on `count()`, top-event selection/ordering may use raw counts while returned timeseries use upsampled counts, making rankings and values inconsistent.

Tests miss high-risk upsampling paths

The endpoint tests cover only simple discover queries with explicit `event.type:error`. They do not cover `dataset=errors`, top events, dashboard split queries, negated/ambiguous event.type conditions, direct use of `upsampled_count()`, or cache expiry/invalidation. These are the paths most likely to expose incorrect counts or query failures.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key construction is ambiguous because fields are joined with underscores

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates namespace, userUID, action, name, and parent using '_' as a separator. Dashboard/folder UIDs can contain underscores, so different combinations of name and parent can produce identical cache keys. For example, name='a_b' with parent='c' yields the same key suffix as name='a' with parent='b_c'. Because this cache stores negative authorization decisions, a key collision can cause a denial for one resource/folder combination to be incorrectly applied to another resource. The key should be constructed with unambiguous escaping/encoding or by hashing the separate fields.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same issue: userPermDenialCacheKey joins its fields with underscores, so keys can collide and produce incorrect denial cache hits. The candidate also gives a concrete collision example.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key omits identity type, allowing denials to leak between identities

userPermDenialCacheKey is built only from namespace, userUID, action, name, and parent folder. validateSubject permits multiple identity types, and different identities can have the same identifier string. For example, 'anonymous:0' and 'render:0' both parse to userUID "0". If an anonymous check for 'dashboards:read' on a dashboard is denied, the denial is cached under a key like ns.perm_0_dashboards:read_<dash>_. A subsequent renderer check for the same dashboard will hit this denial cache at line 117 and be denied before getRendererPermissions can return its built-in read access. The denial cache key must include the identity type (and ideally a normalized internal identity ID) to avoid cross-identity wrongful denials.

Cached denial can persist after permission is granted

When a permission check reaches the database and denies access, the result is cached in permDenialCache for shortCacheTTL (30 seconds). There is no invalidation when permissions change. If the first check for a newly created dashboard/folder happens before the new permission is visible (for example due to read-replica lag or asynchronous permission provisioning), the denial is cached. Subsequent checks within the TTL hit the denial cache and skip the database requery, leaving the creator unable to access the newly created resource for up to the TTL. This reintroduces the same class of staleness problem the PR is trying to fix.

Tests do not cover denial-cache isolation by identity type or grant-after-denial behavior

TestService_CacheCheck only pre-seeds a denial entry for a user and checks that it denies access. It does not verify that denial entries are scoped by identity type, so it would not catch a denial for anonymous affecting the renderer identity. It also does not verify behavior when a permission is granted after a denial has been cached. Since the denial cache is a new authorization decision path, tests should cover cross-identity isolation and stale-denial scenarios.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unsafe access to metadata['sender']['login'] can cause a 500

GitHubInstallation.dispatch compares the OAuth-authenticated user to integration.metadata['sender']['login']. Many legitimate Integration rows may not have metadata.sender (for example, integrations created before this change, installations where the webhook has not populated sender, or first-pass installations as shown in the tests). In those cases this direct subscripting can raise KeyError or TypeError and return a 500 instead of the intended graceful error page. The code should use safe lookups and fail closed when sender login is missing.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same bug: integration.metadata['sender']['login'] is accessed directly, with no check that the sender key exists. That raises a KeyError for integrations whose sender metadata was never set.

false_positives.candidate:
User mismatch validation is skipped when the Integration row does not exist

The new security check only runs after an Integration row exists. When Integration.DoesNotExist is raised, the view returns pipeline.next_step() without verifying that github_authenticated_user matches the installer. If the installation webhook that records sender is delayed, fails, or has not created/updated the Integration yet, the advertised mismatch validation is bypassed and an installation_id could potentially be completed by a different authenticated GitHub user. The flow should fail closed or otherwise verify installer identity before creating the integration.

Query-string installation_id can override the pipeline-bound installation_id

GitHubInstallation.dispatch uses request.GET.get('installation_id', pipeline.fetch_state('installation_id')), which lets a query-string parameter overwrite any installation_id already stored during the OAuth step. This weakens the binding between the GitHub OAuth identity and the installation ID. If an installation_id has already been bound in pipeline state, the view should use that value or require the query parameter to match it rather than silently allowing it to be swapped.

OAuth token exchange omits redirect_uri

The authorization request includes redirect_uri, but the access-token exchange sends only code, client_id, and client_secret. Omitting redirect_uri prevents Sentry from explicitly binding the code exchange to the callback URL used in the authorize step. This matters if the GitHub OAuth app can have multiple callback URLs or if a code could be obtained through another registered redirect URI. The same redirect_uri should be included in the token exchange.

OAuth exchange and user-info fetch can raise 500 instead of showing the intended error

safe_urlopen and get_user_info are called without exception handling; only parsing the response body is wrapped. Network timeouts, connection errors, HTTP errors, or exceptions raised by get_user_info will bubble up and produce a 500 instead of the intended installation-failed error page. The token exchange and user-info fetch should be wrapped and return error() on failure. Also treat an empty access_token as missing, not merely absent.

Authorize redirect URL is built without URL encoding

The GitHub authorize URL is constructed with an f-string, interpolating client_id, state, and redirect_uri directly into the query string. redirect_uri should be URL-encoded to avoid malformed or rejected URLs when reserved characters are present, and to make the construction robust to future changes. Use urllib.parse.urlencode to build the query parameters.

Redirect can be built with installation_id=None

If GitHub redirects with setup_action=install but without an installation_id, installation_id is None and is passed directly to reverse('integration-installation', args=[provider_id, installation_id]). This can generate a URL containing the literal None or cause a reverse/404 failure. The view should handle a missing installation_id with a graceful redirect or error page.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing
OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.

testCacheIDPForLogin creates providers with aliases idp-alias-0 through idp-alias-19 and later idp-alias-20, but registers cleanup for the literal alias instead of the generated alias. The created providers are therefore not removed, leaving test data behind and potentially affecting other tests. The same problem occurs at line 425. Cleanup should use the actual provider alias.

false_positives.candidate:
Login-cache invalidation can be skipped when the original IDP is resolved through an organization-aware wrapper

In update(), the original model is loaded with getById(), which returns an organization-aware IdentityProviderModel whose isEnabled() is false when the linked organization is disabled. registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate() then applies LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate() to this wrapped original. If the organization is disabled, an update that removes login eligibility (for example hideOnLogin=true, linkOnly=true, or broker.public=false) can be evaluated as false -> false and no login-cache invalidation is registered. When the organization is later enabled, the stale getForLogin cache can still contain the provider, and callers that only re-check isEnabled() may display a hidden, private, or link-only provider. Use the raw delegate model for the original state, or invalidate whenever login-related fields change.

getForLogin cache does not react to organization invalidation

getForLogin() checks only isInvalid(cacheKey), where cacheKey is realm+FetchMode. It stores organization-specific result sets inside that mode-level cache entry using organizationId as a search key, but it does not check organization invalidation or otherwise tie the entry to organization lifecycle changes. getByOrganization() at least checks isInvalid(orgId). As a result, organization changes such as enable/disable or update do not refresh these cached login lists, so stale organization-scoped IDP lists can be returned until an unrelated IDP change invalidates the mode key.

Cached getForLogin results are returned without re-validating login eligibility

In the cached path, getForLogin() resolves each cached internal ID and adds the model to the result without verifying that it still satisfies the login criteria (enabled, not link-only, not hidden, and public when organization-linked). The correctness of the cache therefore depends entirely on invalidations being complete. If an invalidation is missed, for example when an IDP is updated while its organization is disabled, this method can return providers that should no longer be available for login. Filtering cached entries before returning them would prevent stale ineligible providers from being exposed.

Mode-level login cache can accumulate unbounded organization search keys

cacheKeyForLogin() is keyed only by realm and FetchMode, while each distinct organizationId queried is stored as another search key inside the same IdentityProviderListQuery. There is no eviction of individual organization search keys; adding a new one invalidates and replaces the whole entry. In realms with many organizations this cached object can grow large and cause extra invalidation/replication overhead. Consider keying by organization or limiting/evicting search keys.

Possible NullPointerException in remove() for a nonexistent alias

remove() fetches storedIdp from the delegate before deletion. If the alias does not exist and isInvalid(cacheKey) is true, storedIdp is null and registerIDPInvalidation(storedIdp) dereferences it, causing a NullPointerException. This can turn removal of a nonexistent alias into an internal error in some cache states. Guard against a null storedIdp before registering invalidation.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
SQL expression gate is hard-coded off and feature-flag logic is misleading

enableSqlExpressions computes enabled as the negation of FlagSqlExpressions but returns false in both branches, so the feature flag has no effect. If the intent is to disable SQL expressions unconditionally for the CVE fix, replace this with an explicit return false and a comment; otherwise the dead toggle logic is misleading and could be incorrectly modified later.

The PR rejects QueryTypeSQL in ReadQuery and stubs the DuckDB implementation, but adds no test verifying that SQL expression queries are rejected, including when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled. A regression test is needed to ensure the vulnerable path cannot be accidentally re-enabled.

If that reload fails, a valid cached value can be replaced with nil; even when it succeeds, it causes redundant disk reads. After acquiring the write lock, re-check `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` and return the existing cached value.

When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:
Asynchronous legacy writes inherit the request context and may be canceled immediately

In Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection, the goroutine that writes to legacy storage derives its context from the incoming request context. When the API request completes, that context is canceled, so the asynchronous legacy create/update/delete/delete-collection can be canceled before it finishes. Mode 3 depends on these asynchronous writes to keep legacy storage in sync, so this can silently drop legacy writes. Use a detached context for the asynchronous operation, preserving only logging/values, not request cancellation.

Legacy update reuses the original UpdatedObjectInfo after it was already used by unified storage

Update calls Storage.Update with the provided rest.UpdatedObjectInfo and then passes the same objInfo to Legacy.Update asynchronously. UpdatedObjectInfo can be request-scoped or one-use, and it may compute the new object from the old object in the store that calls it. Legacy storage may therefore fail, consume an already-consumed payload, or apply the update to a different legacy state, producing a different object than unified storage. For dual-write convergence, legacy should receive the already-updated object returned from Storage.Update, ideally through a wrapper or deep copy.

Delete does not attempt legacy deletion when unified storage returns NotFound

Delete returns immediately if Storage.Delete fails, including when the object is not found in unified storage. In mode 3, legacy storage may still contain a stale copy, and this code path will never clean it up. The previous behavior tolerated NotFound from unified storage and still attempted the legacy delete. Skipping legacy deletion on NotFound can leave divergent legacy objects permanently.

DeleteCollection does not attempt legacy deletion when unified storage returns an error

DeleteCollection returns immediately if Storage.DeleteCollection fails, so Legacy.DeleteCollection is not attempted. If unified storage reports an error or has already removed the collection while legacy storage still contains objects, the legacy data will remain and the stores will diverge. For mode 3 dual-write cleanup, legacy deletion should still be attempted where appropriate, especially when the unified store reports the collection is already absent.

Async legacy create uses the original object without copying it

Create passes the same runtime.Object pointer to the asynchronous Legacy.Create call that was passed to Storage.Create. Storage implementations commonly mutate the object during create, and legacy storage may also mutate it. Returning to the caller while a background goroutine continues to use or mutate the same object can cause data races and inconsistent objects. The object should be deep-copied before being handed to the asynchronous legacy writer.

Storage create failure is recorded as a legacy-store duration

When Storage.Create fails, Create records the duration with recordLegacyDuration using the storage start time. This reports a unified-storage failure under legacy-store metrics, making storage and legacy latency/error metrics incorrect. It should call recordStorageDuration.

Storage update failure is recorded as a legacy-store duration

When Storage.Update fails, Update records the duration with recordLegacyDuration using the storage start time. This mislabels unified-storage update failures as legacy-store update failures. It should call recordStorageDuration.

Legacy delete-collection duration is recorded as a storage duration

In the asynchronous DeleteCollection goroutine, the result of Legacy.DeleteCollection is recorded with recordStorageDuration. This reports legacy-store delete-collection latency/errors under unified-storage metrics. It should call recordLegacyDuration.

Every write starts an unbounded goroutine for legacy replication

Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection each start a new goroutine for the legacy write. There is no queue, worker pool, semaphore, or other backpressure mechanism. If legacy storage is slow or unavailable, write traffic can create a large number of blocked goroutines, increasing memory use and potentially destabilizing the process.

Destroy does not wait for outstanding asynchronous legacy writes

Destroy closes both Storage and Legacy immediately, but mode 3 may still have outstanding goroutines calling Legacy.Create, Legacy.Update, Legacy.Delete, or Legacy.DeleteCollection. Those goroutines can then operate on destroyed storage, causing errors or panics. The dual writer should track outstanding asynchronous writes and wait for them, or at least cancel and drain them, during Destroy.

Asynchronous legacy write failures are not logged

The asynchronous legacy paths only record metrics when the legacy operation fails; they no longer log the error. Since mode 3 returns success to the client as soon as unified storage succeeds, legacy failures are otherwise invisible. This makes diagnosing divergence between unified and legacy storage difficult. Errors from asynchronous legacy writes should be logged, ideally with the object identity and operation.

Unit tests do not synchronize with or verify asynchronous legacy writes

Mode 3 methods start background goroutines, but the unit tests return immediately after calling Create, Delete, Update, or DeleteCollection. There is no WaitGroup, channel, or injectable executor to wait for the legacy call. Some tests set legacy mock expectations but never assert them, while Delete and DeleteCollection do not set legacy expectations at all, so background mock calls may occur after the test finishes or panic as unexpected calls. These tests do not reliably prove that legacy writes happen.

Mode 3 integration test assumes immediate legacy consistency despite asynchronous writes

The new mode 3 integration test runs the same playlist CRUD suite, which creates/updates/deletes objects through the Kubernetes API and then immediately checks the legacy API. In mode 3, legacy writes are asynchronous, so the legacy API may not yet reflect the change. Without polling/eventual-consistency waits, this test can be flaky and may fail or pass for timing reasons rather than correctness.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

copyToClipboard calls navigator.clipboard?.writeText(text).then(...) without a catch handler. If the clipboard write fails, the promise rejection is unhandled and the user receives no feedback. A rejection handler should be added, ideally with an error toast or fallback.

GrafanaGroupLoader's comment says it loads an evaluation group from Prometheus and Ruler endpoints, but the ruler query was removed in this PR. The component now only polls the Prometheus endpoint. The comment and the nearby expectedRulesCount comment referencing Ruler responses should be updated.

Sharded queries are interpolated twice

runShardSplitQuery() maps every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables() at line 52, then later executes each shard group through runSplitQuery(). runSplitQuery() was changed to also map every incoming target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables() in querySplitting.ts line 299. As a result, sharded expressions are interpolated again after the __stream_shard__ matcher has been injected. The added test even expects five interpolation calls for one target. Template interpolation is not guaranteed to be idempotent; repeated calls can duplicate ad-hoc filters or reinterpret variable syntax introduced by the first interpolation. Interpolation should be performed in only one layer.

runSplitQuery() filters targets on query.expr before calling applyTemplateVariables(). If a raw expression is a template variable that resolves to an empty string, the target passes the non-empty filter, becomes empty after interpolation, and is still grouped and sent to Loki. This can create invalid empty queries. Add a non-empty expr filter after interpolation; the same problem exists in runShardSplitQuery().

runShardSplitQuery() filters request.targets by the raw query.expr before interpolation. A target whose expression is a variable that expands to an empty string will still enter splitQueriesByStreamShard(), potentially causing shard-label lookups for an empty selector and sending an empty query downstream. Targets should be filtered again after applyTemplateVariables().

Under concurrent requests from new device IDs, multiple callers can observe count < deviceLimit and all insert, causing the stored active device count to exceed the configured limit.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.

Failed device tagging is cached, allowing device-limit bypass

tagDeviceUI stores the device ID in localCache before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice and does not remove it when CreateOrUpdateDevice fails. If the database returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, the first request is rejected, but the cache entry remains for about 29 minutes. A retry with the same X-Grafana-Device-Id hits the cache, tagDeviceUI returns nil, Anonymous.Authenticate succeeds, and the device is allowed despite never being admitted under the limit. This makes the configurable limit ineffective after one failed retry per device ID and also masks transient DB errors.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same issue. tagDeviceUI caches the device ID before CreateOrUpdateDevice, and the entry persists after ErrDeviceLimitReached. That lets the device bypass the limit for about 29 minutes.

false_positives.candidate:

Anonymous.Authenticate now calls TagDevice synchronously. When device_limit is enabled and a device is not in the local cache, this executes a COUNT over anon_device plus an insert/update before authentication completes. Unique device IDs can force this path on every request, adding latency to anonymous logins and creating a DB load vector that did not exist when tagging ran asynchronously with a timeout.

Missing X-Grafana-Device-Id bypasses the device limit

TagDevice returns nil immediately when the X-Grafana-Device-Id header is absent, and Anonymous.Authenticate then returns an anonymous identity. Because the limit is only enforced for requests that supply this client-controlled header, a client can avoid being counted or blocked simply by omitting the header. If the limit is intended to cap anonymous access, this is a bypass.

untagDevice logs the wrong error variable

When anonStore.DeleteDevice fails, untagDevice logs the outer err variable, which has already been checked to be nil, instead of errD returned by DeleteDevice. The resulting log message does not contain the actual deletion error.

Negative device_limit is silently treated as unlimited

AnonymousDeviceLimit is read with MustInt64(0), and anonstore only enforces the limit when deviceLimit > 0. A negative configuration value therefore disables limiting instead of being rejected or clamped to zero, which can hide operator mistakes.

No tests cover device-limit enforcement and cache interaction

The updated tests use setting.NewCfg(), whose AnonymousDeviceLimit defaults to 0, and assert TagDevice never errors. There is no test that a limit-reached failure is returned consistently on retries, that the local cache does not mask a failed create, or that existing active devices can still update when the limit is reached.

On first concurrent use, multiple threads can race on assignment; one thread can overwrite the array after another has recorded loaded locales, causing duplicate locale loading or transient inconsistent state. Initialization and checks of @loaded_locales should be done under LOAD_MUTEX or through a synchronized memoized accessor.

false_positives.candidate:
Translation cache key ignores dynamic fallback chain

The LRU cache key only contains the translation key, current locale, and backend object id. This PR makes fallback resolution depend on SiteSetting.default_locale (and always :en). If two requests use the same I18n.locale but have different default locales (for example in multisite, or after an admin changes default_locale without a full I18n cache clear), a fallback translation cached for one context can be returned for another, serving the wrong language until the cache is cleared or evicted. Include the fallback chain/default locale/site identifier in the cache key, or invalidate this cache when fallback inputs change.

Fallback locales are only ensured loaded for controller requests

I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded! is called only in ApplicationController#set_locale. The translate accelerator lazily loads only the current locale inside I18n.translate, so fallback target locales (site default and :en) are not loaded in mailers, Sidekiq jobs, rake tasks, console, middleware, or any code path that translates without passing through this controller filter. In those contexts, missing translations will not fall back and may return translation-missing strings or raise instead. Fallback locales should be ensured whenever I18n.locale is set or inside the translate path.

translate still assumes @loaded_locales is initialized

The new ensure_loaded! method initializes @loaded_locales, but translate still calls @loaded_locales.include?(config.locale) without initializing it. If any code calls I18n.translate before ensure_loaded!, reload!, or load_locale has run, this will raise NoMethodError on nil. translate should use a memoized/synchronized accessor or initialize @loaded_locales before checking it.

No tests for new fallback/loading behavior

This PR changes global I18n fallback order, lazy locale loading, and request-time loading, but adds no specs covering: missing translations falling back to SiteSetting.default_locale and :en; loading of fallback locales outside controllers; or cache invalidation when default_locale changes. Without tests, regressions in fallback behavior or cache staleness are likely.
